titulo.texto: Lacandon Clay Incense Burner and Censer

frase_gancho.texto: A clay face through which the Lacandon speak with their gods.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the rainforest we travel north, to the Yucatán Peninsula. Look for a white three-piece dress, embroidered with large, colorful flowers and finished with lace.

guion_corto.texto: This clay vessel is an incense burner of the Lacandon, who call themselves hach winik, “the true people,” and live in the rainforest of Chiapas. It is modeled by hand, without a wheel, and on the front it bears the face of a deity, with marked eyebrows, round eyes, and bands painted in white and red. Copal is burned inside, and offerings of food are placed in it. The fragrant smoke rises toward the sky and works as a message: this is how the Lacandon give thanks for their sustenance, ask for health for their families, and speak with Hachakyum, their creator god. For them, an incense burner is not a simple utensil. It is a presence that receives the offering and listens.

guion_largo.texto:
“Lacandon” is the name given to them by outsiders; they call themselves hach winik, “the true people.” Their language is very similar to the Maya spoken in Yucatán, even though they live many kilometers from there, in the rainforest of eastern Chiapas, one of the largest that Mexico has left. They are a small people, of around a thousand persons, spread across communities such as Nahá, Metzabok, and Lacanjá Chansayab.

For them, the gods have a house of their own: the house of the gods, a simple structure of wood and palm, set apart from the family homes. This is where the incense burners are kept, and they are much more than vessels. In the renewal ceremonies they are offered food and drink, as if they were guests: corn dough and balché, a fermented drink made from tree bark and honey. It is said that each incense burner comes to life when it is consecrated, and that it grows old with the years.

Copal is the voice of the ceremony. It is the resin of a tree, and in several Maya languages it is called pom. You already saw it in the [Otomí oratory](mna_s15_oratorio_familiar) and in the [Xantolo altar](mna_s18_altar_xantolo): all across Mexico, the smoke of copal is a bridge to the sacred. Among the Maya it is extremely ancient, and it is thought that the temples you saw downstairs were filled with this very same smoke more than a thousand years ago.

Places tell stories too. Yaxchilán, the city of the [lintel](mna_s09_dintel26_yaxchilan) that you saw in the Maya Hall downstairs, is for the Lacandon a dwelling place of their gods, and it is said that for a long time they traveled all the way there to burn copal. From that relationship comes a curious anecdote: the paintings of Bonampak were made known to the world in nineteen forty-six, and it is said that a Lacandon guide led an American photographer to them.

Look at the face calmly. The thick eyebrows, the round eyes, and the open mouth give it a watchful air, as if the clay were looking back at whoever looks at it. If you move closer, you will notice painted geometric bands and the wear left by the hands that held it. An incense burner like this is not made in a hurry: it takes its ritual, its prayer, and its time.

Lacandon elders have said that as long as there are ceremonies and the incense burners are renewed, the sky will stay in its place, and that if the ritual were forgotten, the world could come to an end. It is a very powerful way of saying something simple: tradition holds up the universe. It also helps us understand why such a small people has taken such care of its ceremonies.

Today the rainforest is changing fast, with roads, cattle ranching, and tourism, and caring for the ceremonies is part of caring for a way of life. That is why an object like this is so valuable: it is not just a pretty piece of clay, but a testimony to how a people converses with its world.

From the cold of the Highlands to the heat of the rainforest is barely a day’s journey, but the clothing, the food, and the gods all change. What remains is the gesture of giving thanks, of giving something in return for what one receives, with smoke, with food, or with words.

texto: Look for the face modeled on the front: eyebrows, eyes, and mouth
Observe the bands painted in white and red
Imagine the copal smoke rising out of the opening

texto.Region: Lacandon Jungle (Nahá, Mensäbäk, and Frontera Corozal, Chiapas)
texto.Technique/Material: Hand-modeled clay, plant-based paint (achiote), and copal resin
texto.Function: Sacred vessel for the ritual burning of copal and for feeding the deities

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient Maya disappeared and their ceremonies were lost.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Lacandon, a people of the rainforest of Chiapas, still burn copal in clay incense burners to speak with their gods.
